questions.q: What real analogy did the instructor use to explain what a mapping is?
options: A phone book or dictionary — a key (like a name) mapped to a value (like a phone number)
A vending machine
A stack of plates
A traffic light
questions.explain: A mapping was compared directly to a phone book: each key (a name) is mapped to a specific value (a phone number).

questions.q: What does calling `remove` (which uses `delete`) actually do to a mapping?
options: Resets that one key's value back to its default — it doesn't erase the whole mapping
Deletes every key-value pair in the entire mapping
Permanently deletes the mapping's type declaration
Has no real effect on a mapping
questions.explain: delete only resets the value at the specified key back to its default (e.g., 0 for a uint256) — the mapping itself and its other entries are untouched.

questions.q: Why can't you loop through all the entries in a mapping, per this lesson?
options: Mappings only store values, not a list of keys — Solidity has no way to iterate them
Loops are disabled entirely in Solidity
You actually can loop through them freely
Mappings can only ever hold a single key
questions.explain: A real, explicit limitation: mappings don't store keys, only values, so Solidity provides no built-in way to loop through all of a mapping's entries.

questions.q: What does `mapping(address => mapping(uint256 => bool)) public nested;` actually represent?
options: A mapping where each address points to another mapping, which maps a uint256 to a bool
Three completely separate, unrelated mappings
An array of addresses
A syntax error — mappings cannot be nested
questions.explain: This is a real nested mapping: an address key leads to a second mapping, whose own keys are uint256 values mapped to booleans.

questions.q: Why is `mapping(address => uint256) public myMap;` described as the foundation for the rest of this chapter?
options: It's the exact real structure a token contract uses to track each account's balance
It has no real connection to token standards
It's only used for testing, never in production contracts
It replaces the need for a constructor
questions.explain: An address mapped to a uint256 is precisely the pattern a token's balance tracker uses — every account's holdings, keyed by their address.
